title: Bronchiolitis — Evaluation & Management
keywords: clinical diagnosis do not order CXR or viral testing routinely
supportive care oxygen suction hydration is the treatment

ageRange: Typically infants and children < 2 years, peak incidence 2-6 months; classic RSV season but caused by multiple respiratory viruses
purpose: How to diagnose and manage bronchiolitis without over-testing or over-treating — this is a clinical diagnosis, and the single most common management error is ordering tests or giving medications the evidence says don't help.

body.text: Diagnosis — clinical, not radiographic or laboratory

Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis: an upper respiratory prodrome (rhinorrhea, congestion) followed by lower respiratory findings — wheeze, crackles, tachypnea, increased work of breathing — in a child under 2. Do NOT routinely order a chest X-ray or viral testing (RSV/respiratory panel) for a typical presentation — imaging findings are nonspecific and frequently drive unnecessary antibiotic use for what is a viral illness, and a positive or negative viral test rarely changes management for an individual patient.

Reserve chest X-ray for atypical presentations: focal findings suggesting a complication (pneumonia, effusion), a toxic-appearing child, or a diagnosis in question — not as a routine part of the bronchiolitis workup.
What does NOT help — the core of the guideline

items: Albuterol/albuterol or other bronchodilators — not recommended, even as a therapeutic trial. Studies consistently fail to show benefit, and treating anyway delays recognition that the wheeze isn't reversible bronchospasm.
Systemic corticosteroids — not recommended for isolated bronchiolitis (distinct from wheeze with an asthma/reactive-airway component in an older child).
Nebulized hypertonic saline — evidence is mixed/inconsistent; not routinely recommended, particularly not in the ED for a brief encounter.
Antibiotics — not indicated unless a specific concurrent bacterial infection (e.g. otitis media, pneumonia) is identified; bronchiolitis itself is viral.
Chest physiotherapy — not shown to help and not recommended.
Nasal suctioning — the single most useful intervention for a congested infant, especially before feeds and before reassessing work of breathing.

Supplemental oxygen for hypoxemia — a specific universal SpO2 cutoff for treatment is not mandated by the guideline; use clinical status and trend rather than chasing a number in an otherwise well infant with borderline saturations.
Maintain hydration — many infants feed poorly from nasal congestion and tachypnea; IV or NG fluids for those unable to maintain oral intake.

Monitor for apnea — a real risk in young infants (particularly < 2 months corrected age or ex-premature infants), even before major respiratory distress develops; this drives admission decisions independent of oxygen requirement.

body.text: High-flow nasal cannula — a genuinely evolving question

HFNC is effective rescue therapy for an infant failing standard low-flow oxygen, but the evidence does not support routine, early, liberal use as a default first-line therapy for mild-to-moderate distress — starting HFNC too early/too broadly has been associated with longer hospital stays without a clear outcome benefit over standard oxygen in infants who don't need it.

Practice variation in exactly when to start, how to titrate, and when to wean HFNC remains substantial enough that a 2026 Delphi/RAND-UCLA appropriateness consensus was published specifically to address it.

Follow your institution's protocol for specific flow rates and escalation/weaning criteria rather than a fixed number here.

items: Hypoxemia not correctable with low-flow oxygen, or an escalating oxygen/respiratory-support requirement
Significant work of breathing (retractions, grunting, nasal flaring) or apnea
Young age (especially < 2-3 months) or ex-premature infant with apnea risk, even with otherwise mild findings
Underlying risk factors: chronic lung disease, hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease
